description: We are The Last BrainCell, a team of BUET CSE undergrads representing Dhaka in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. we are designing an interactive simulation that teaches young minds about space exploration and astronaut life.
summary: Last Light Academy is a free, offline, open-source 3D mission trainer for ages 10–15 on Windows and macOS. It answers “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” by putting up to four learners on one computer in charge of Aurora Station at the Moon’s south pole. To survive a 36-hour training night and help Alo, a small mustard plant, live to bloom, they balance life support, radiation shielding, power and food production. Every plan can be previewed with “Try it” before commitment: the water shielding the crew from a replay of the 10 September 2017 solar storm is also the water Alo needs. Across eight chapters, 32 missions and 96 scenes, 16 science puzzles turn these trade-offs into decisions players must explain. The game bundles 29 NASA and other scientific source extracts offline; Data Cards distinguish observed values, calculations and training assumptions. Solo play and shared-computer Class mode make hands-on space science accessible without internet or accounts.
details:
WHAT WE BUILT

Last Light Academy is a free, offline, open-source 3D mission trainer for ages 10–15 on Windows and macOS. Up to four learners share one computer to run Aurora Station at the Moon’s south pole. Their mission is to protect four cadets and keep Alo, a Brassica rapa mustard plant, alive until she can bloom.

THE CHALLENGE AND WHY IT MATTERS

“Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” asks students to balance life support, radiation shielding, power and food production. Our game makes those competing needs tangible: the electricity that warms the crew also makes their air; the water protecting them from radiation also feeds their plants. Designed by a team in Bangladesh, it brings practical space-science activities to learners with limited connectivity, using one shared computer and no account or specialist equipment.

HOW IT WORKS

Four cadets divide responsibility: Kai manages power and heat, Amara air, Mei the garden and Rafi space weather. At the Mission Table they plan seven 7.2-hour shifts: two in daylight, then five through an authored 36-hour night. Players set heating, oxygen production, garden lighting and water allocation. “Try it” previews a plan using the same simulation that executes it; “Lock in” commits the decision.

The four demands stay connected:

• Life support: a 10-unit air tank; four crew consume one unit per shift, and oxygen production uses power. NASA BVAD’s 0.895 kg O₂/person/day gives approximately 1.07 kg per game air unit.

• Radiation shielding: pump water into the shelter wall, stack supply crates or wait. The full-wall teaching model represents 20 g/cm² of water, informed by NASA shielding research.

• Power: a 20-unit battery gains eight units per daylight shift and none in darkness, with its scale informed by NASA’s 10 kW solar-array study.

• Food production: rations and the garden share the station’s resources; grow lights use electricity and plants need water also used for shielding.

Solo play gives one player all four roles. In Class mode, 2–4 learners share role-specific information, and decisions require all four roles to sign off. A shift-by-shift replay and predict–observe–explain debrief connect forecasts, choices and outcomes. Four endings and checkpoint retries make mistakes opportunities to learn.

The campaign spans eight chapters, 32 missions and 96 scenes across one lunar seasonal cycle. Its 16 science puzzles cover pollination, moonquake damage, cold-trap exploration, impact flashes, the 12 January 2047 eclipse, storm sheltering and restoring a relay link to Earth.

NASA DATA AT THE CORE

The game bundles 29 scientific source extracts offline. Python scripts retrieve original records or preserve values from cited papers, with source URLs or DOIs, retrieval details and documented calculations. NASA DONKI supplies event timing for the September 2017 storm replay; NOAA GOES-13 supplies Earth-orbit proton observations. NASA BVAD, shielding and solar-array studies anchor resource models. LRO LOLA elevation data shapes the terrain, while JPL Horizons supplies Sun and Earth geometry. NASA OSDR, Apollo seismic records, LCROSS, Diviner and the eclipse catalog support later missions.

Data Cards distinguish Observed, Computed and Training assumption values. The outpost, characters and 36-hour scenario are authored; resource units and radiation responses are simplified teaching models. GOES observations are not lunar-surface measurements. The July 2012 storm reaching the Moon is explicitly a “what if”. Learners can inspect both the evidence and the model’s limits.

ACCESSIBILITY AND DEVELOPMENT

Captions, text scaling to 1.5×, reduced motion, guided objectives and optional hints support different learners. The project includes 386 voiced lines, 18 cutscenes and 41 narrated clips: 22 how-to films and 19 science explainers. Its repository contains 141 automated test suites covering game systems and campaign routes.

We used Godot 4.7, GDScript and shaders; Python with NumPy; Blender; FFmpeg; gohud; Playwright; and GitHub Actions. The team created the concept, story, characters and puzzle specifications, directed the art and reviewed the work. AI assisted code, assets, media, supporting text and documentation. Our code is Apache-2.0 licensed; external materials retain their licences.

INTENDED IMPACT AND NEXT STEPS

We aim to build systems thinking, scientific reasoning and teamwork in school labs, clubs, libraries and homes. Alo connects the mission to Bangladesh’s familiar winter mustard fields. Next we plan Bangla text and voices, classroom evaluation of prediction and explanation skills, and more missions. Mars, mobile and online co-op are future ambitions.
